loro-piana.origin: Loro Piana is a Biella textile maison and cloth brand, not a fiber species. It is widely associated with fine wool and cashmere products. Cashmere still comes from goats (Capra hircus subtypes used for undercoat); wool from sheep. Spinning, weaving and finishing may be described in Biella-district language on producer pages. This entry is a teaching reference for mill-maison provenance. It does not invent map edges or certify Storm System or other finishes beyond producer documentation.
loro-piana.structure: The maison name does not create a new polymer or keratin. Cashmere remains fine undercoat hair; merino and other wools remain sheep keratin with measurable mean diameter. Branded cloth collections and finishes (for example producer-documented Storm System weather finishes) are commercial product systems layered on those fibers. Read the fiber-content line and any finish care notes for the actual composition.
loro-piana.process: A textile maison may comb, spin, weave and finish in-house or with partners, then sell cloth and finished goods. Biella signals a processing geography often used in marketing; farm geography can be Australia, New Zealand, Mongolia, China or elsewhere depending on the fiber. Storm System and similar names should be checked on the producer’s technical or product pages for the specific cloth, not generalized to every Loro Piana label.
loro-piana.performance: Fine cashmere and high Super S wool cloths are valued for hand and drape; they are not automatically more durable. Producer weather finishes claim water and wind resistance on documented fabrics; those claims are producer statements requiring the finish name on the product. Pilling, abrasion and wet strength depend on yarn, weave and finish. Prestige does not replace a care label.
loro-piana.identify: No lab test names Loro Piana. Microscopy distinguishes wool and cashmere with limits; DNA or protein methods exist in specialist labs. Labels and selvedge tickets identify the maison. Pecora Nera and other collection names, when used in public stories, are mill-cloth designations rather than generic fiber classes.
loro-piana.labeling: Cashmere and wool labeling follow national wool and textile fiber rules (for example US 16 CFR Part 300 and EU 1007/2011). Specialty collection names are trademarks or product names. Finish trademarks such as Storm System are not fiber names and should not replace the generic fiber disclosure.
loro-piana.past: Loro Piana’s public narrative is a family Biella textile business that later became a global luxury maison (including ownership changes reported in the business press). Use producer and serious trade histories for dates; the atlas emphasizes fiber-versus-maison distinctions rather than corporate timelines.

piacenza-1733.origin: Piacenza 1733 (Fratelli Piacenza) is a historic Biella-area wool mill house based in Pollone, Italy. The producer publicly dates its founding to 1733. It is not a fiber species. Wool still comes from sheep raised in wool-growing regions worldwide; the mill house name marks processing and design heritage in the Biella district. This atlas entry teaches mill-house provenance. It adds no map supplier edges.
piacenza-1733.structure: Mill-house branding does not alter keratin structure. Merino and other wools remain diameter-graded sheep fibers; blends follow each component. Historic mill collections may emphasize noble fibers and seasonal cloth weights. Always separate the mill trademark from the generic fiber name on the label.
piacenza-1733.process: A vertical or semi-vertical wool mill may scour, card or comb, spin, weave and finish under one house identity, or coordinate stages with partners. Biella district clustering historically supported that chain. Producer sustainability and heritage pages describe current practice; treat them as attributed claims. Farm-to-mill logistics are not inferred by this atlas.
piacenza-1733.performance: Cloth performance follows yarn count, weave, weight and finish. A three-century founding date does not guarantee a particular hand or durability on every modern SKU. Compare GSM, weave and care instructions across products. Marketing about authenticity should be read beside measurable cloth specs.
piacenza-1733.identify: No microscopy test identifies Piacenza 1733. Labels, selvedges and swing tickets identify the mill house. Country-of-origin marking may show Italy for weaving or make-up while fiber origin differs. Ask for the fiber content and any mill ticket codes when studying a cloth.
piacenza-1733.labeling: Wool labeling rules still govern fiber names and percentages. The mill-house trademark is additional commercial information. EU and US fiber regulations do not replace care labels. Heritage dates on marketing sites are not legal fiber designations.
piacenza-1733.past: The producer states a 1733 founding in Pollone in the Biella district and membership narratives such as long-lived family business associations on its public story pages. Use those producer pages for heritage claims. The atlas cites them to illustrate how mill houses market continuity, not to audit every historical episode.
facts: Historic Biella wool mill house (trademark), not a fiber

paul-smith.origin: Paul Smith is a British designer menswear house, not a fiber, sheep breed or mill trademark for a keratin. Public product stories often name cloth and make details, while the fiber itself still comes from farms and mills named on labels and tickets. This atlas treats the trademark as educational vocabulary for reading hangtags, mill cloth names and generic fiber classes without certifying supply chains, performance claims or animal welfare.
paul-smith.structure: Nothing in the Paul Smith name changes wool chemistry. Suiting and shirting remain wool, cotton or stated blends specified per product, with yarn twist, weave and finish set by the cloth supplier rather than by the designer trademark. This atlas treats the trademark as educational vocabulary for reading hangtags, mill cloth names and generic fiber classes without certifying supply chains, performance claims or animal welfare.
paul-smith.process: A designer house typically specifies cloth and silhouette, then cuts and sews garments through its manufacturing network. Educational value is reading hangtags for fiber content, mill cloth names and country of make separately from the designer label on the jacket. This atlas treats the trademark as educational vocabulary for reading hangtags, mill cloth names and generic fiber classes without certifying supply chains, performance claims or animal welfare.
paul-smith.performance: Performance belongs to the specified cloth and construction, not to the house name alone. Crease recovery, breathability and durability track fiber grade, yarn, weave and finishing choices documented for each SKU. This atlas treats the trademark as educational vocabulary for reading hangtags, mill cloth names and generic fiber classes without certifying supply chains, performance claims or animal welfare.
paul-smith.identify: No laboratory test identifies Paul Smith as a material. Microscopy and diameter measurement characterize wool; burning tests and solubility methods help sort cellulosic and synthetic fibers when labels are missing or incomplete. This atlas treats the trademark as educational vocabulary for reading hangtags, mill cloth names and generic fiber classes without certifying supply chains, performance claims or animal welfare.
paul-smith.labeling: In the United States, wool products follow 16 CFR Part 300; in the EU, fiber names follow Regulation (EU) No 1007/2011. The designer trademark does not replace generic fiber names on the legal composition panel. This atlas treats the trademark as educational vocabulary for reading hangtags, mill cloth names and generic fiber classes without certifying supply chains, performance claims or animal welfare.
paul-smith.past: Paul Smith developed as a British designer brand with a long menswear and cloth-aware retail presence. Exact founding anecdotes belong to producer histories rather than fiber science, so this atlas keeps the chronology light and attributed. This atlas treats the trademark as educational vocabulary for reading hangtags, mill cloth names and generic fiber classes without certifying supply chains, performance claims or animal welfare.

wool and other fibers as labeled per garment
